claim: Early social deprivation reduced social preference in juvenile zebrafish.
source: As in humans and other social species, early social deprivation reduced social preference in juvenile zebrafish.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Whole-brain functional maps of anti-social isolated (lonely) fish were distinct from anti-social (loner) fish found in the normal population.
source: Whole-brain functional maps of anti-social isolated (lonely) fish were distinct from anti-social (loner) fish found in the normal population.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Isolation-induced activity changes revealed profound disruption of neural activity in brain areas linked to social behaviour, social cue processing, and anxiety/stress.
source: These isolation-induced activity changes revealed profound disruption of neural activity in brain areas linked to social behaviour, social cue processing, and anxiety/stress.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Several of the affected regions are modulated by serotonin.
source: Several of the affected regions are modulated by serotonin, and we found that social preference in isolated fish could be rescued by acutely reducing serotonin levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Social preference in isolated fish could be rescued by acutely reducing serotonin levels.
source: Several of the affected regions are modulated by serotonin, and we found that social preference in isolated fish could be rescued by acutely reducing serotonin levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Most zebrafish develop a strong social preference by 2–3 weeks of age.
source: We previously found that most zebrafish develop a strong social preference by 2–3 weeks of age (Dreosti et al., 2015), yet we also found a small number (~10%) of 'loner' fish that were averse to social cues.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Approximately 10% of zebrafish are 'loner' fish that are averse to social cues.
source: We previously found that most zebrafish develop a strong social preference by 2–3 weeks of age (Dreosti et al., 2015), yet we also found a small number (~10%) of 'loner' fish that were averse to social cues.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: A similar diversity of individual social preferences has been found in many species, including humans.
source: A similar diversity of individual social preferences has been found in many species, including humans (Sloan Wilson et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Loneliness has been linked to a reduction in social preference.
source: Loneliness, undesired isolation from social interaction, has been linked to a reduction in social preference (Engeszer et al., 2004; Shams et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Isolation induces patterns of brain activity that are not present in the normal population.
source: This comparison found that isolation induces patterns of brain activity that are not present in the normal population.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Some of the highly activated areas in isolated fish are serotoninergic.
source: Since some of the highly activated areas in isolated fish are serotoninergic, we used Buspirone, a 5HT1A receptor agonist.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Prolonged periods of social isolation are particularly detrimental to humans during early development.
source: Prolonged periods of social isolation are particularly detrimental to humans during early development.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Even brief periods of social isolation have been shown to impact mental and physical health.
source: However, even brief periods of social isolation have been shown to impact mental and physical health.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Full social isolation caused a significant decrease in social preference relative to normally raised sibling controls (p=8.3e−8).
source: Full social isolation (Fi) caused a significant decrease in social preference relative to normally raised sibling controls (C) (Figure 1A, left and middle panel: C vs Fi, p=8.3e−8, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1A.

claim: Full social isolation caused an increase in the number of individuals that had a large negative VPI.
source: Specifically, there was an increase in the number of individuals that had a large negative VPI.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Fish that underwent Partial isolation exhibited an intermediate, yet highly significant, change in social preference (p=2.5e−8).
source: Fish that underwent Partial isolation (Pi), exhibited an intermediate, yet highly significant, change in social preference (Figure 1A, right panel: C vs Pi, p=2.5e−8, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1A.

claim: Fish raised in isolation were significantly less active than their normally raised siblings during the acclimation period.
source: As previously reported (Zellner et al., 2011), we found that fish raised in isolation were significantly less active than their normally raised siblings during the acclimation period (Figure 1B: C vs Fi, p=9.0e−6; C vs Pi, p=2.8e-9 Mann-Whitney)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis, Figure 1B, and a citation to previous work.

claim: Fish raised in isolation were significantly less active than their normally raised siblings during the social viewing session.
source: As previously reported (Zellner et al., 2011), we found that fish raised in isolation were significantly less active than their normally raised siblings during the acclimation period (Figure 1B: C vs Fi, p=9.0e−6; C vs Pi, p=2.8e-9 Mann-Whitney) and during the social viewing session (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A: left C vs Fi, p=0.0001; C vs Pi, p=0.004 Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Anti-social fully and partially isolated fish showed very similar movement activity compared to anti-social controls during the acclimation.
source: Interestingly, anti-social fully and partially isolated fish showed very similar movement activity compared to anti-social controls during the acclimation (Figure 1C left: C (-S) vs Fi (-S), p=0.17 Mann-Whitney; C (-S) vs Pi (-S) p=0.23 Mann-Whitney)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1C.

claim: Anti-social fully and partially isolated fish showed very similar movement activity compared to anti-social controls during the social viewing session.
source: Interestingly, anti-social fully and partially isolated fish showed very similar movement activity compared to anti-social controls during the acclimation (Figure 1C left: C (-S) vs Fi (-S), p=0.17 Mann-Whitney; C (-S) vs Pi (-S) p=0.23 Mann-Whitney) and during the social viewing session (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B left: C (-S) vs Fi (-S), p=0.48 Mann-Whitney; C (-S) vs Pi (-S) p=0.10 Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pro-social isolated fish exhibited a reduction in activity relative to controls during the acclimation session.
source: The pro-social isolated fish, which also exhibited a reduction in activity relative to controls during the acclimation session (Figure 1C right: C (-S) vs Fi (-S), p=8.0e−5 Mann-Whitney; C (-S) vs Pi (-S) p=1.0e−7 Mann-Whitney)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1C.

claim: Pro-social isolated fish showed similar activity relative to controls during social viewing.
source: The pro-social isolated fish, which also exhibited a reduction in activity relative to controls during the acclimation session (Figure 1C right: C (-S) vs Fi (-S), p=8.0e−5 Mann-Whitney; C (-S) vs Pi (-S) p=1.0e−7 Mann-Whitney), instead showed similar activity relative to controls during social viewing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B right: C (-S) vs Fi (-S), p=0.02 Mann-Whitney; C (-S) vs Pi (-S) p=0.14 Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All isolated fish behaved qualitatively differently, exhibiting prolonged periods of quiescence (freezing) even when observing conspecifics.
source: In addition, we noticed that all isolated fish behaved qualitatively differently, exhibiting prolonged periods of quiescence (freezing) even when observing conspecifics (Figure 1D and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1D and Video 1.

claim: Freezing is a hallmark of anxiety-like behaviour observed in many species.
source: Freezing is a hallmark of anxiety-like behaviour observed in many species, and reported in zebrafish exposed to stressors (Giacomini et al., 2015; Shams et al., 2018), including periods of social isolation (Egan et al., 2009; Shams et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Freezing has been reported in zebrafish exposed to stressors, including periods of social isolation.
source: Freezing is a hallmark of anxiety-like behaviour observed in many species, and reported in zebrafish exposed to stressors (Giacomini et al., 2015; Shams et al., 2018), including periods of social isolation (Egan et al., 2009; Shams et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both fully and partially isolated fish exhibited significantly more freezing than controls during the acclimation period.
source: We found that both fully and partially isolated fish exhibited significantly more freezing than controls during the acclimation period (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C left: C vs Fi, p=3.4e−16 Mann-Whitney; C vs Pi, p=2.8e−5 Mann-Whitney)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The increase in freezing relative to controls persisted for fully isolated fish during social viewing.
source: We found that both fully and partially isolated fish exhibited significantly more freezing than controls during the acclimation period (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C left: C vs Fi, p=3.4e−16 Mann-Whitney; C vs Pi, p=2.8e−5 Mann-Whitney), and that this increase relative to controls persisted for fully isolated fish during social viewing, but was reduced in partially isolated fish, perhaps representing some recovery during the 15 min of social interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D left: C vs Fi, p=6.3e−13 Mann-Whitney; C vs Pi, p=0.03 Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The increase in freezing was reduced in partially isolated fish during social viewing, perhaps representing some recovery during the 15 min of social interaction.
source: We found that both fully and partially isolated fish exhibited significantly more freezing than controls during the acclimation period (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C left: C vs Fi, p=3.4e−16 Mann-Whitney; C vs Pi, p=2.8e−5 Mann-Whitney), and that this increase relative to controls persisted for fully isolated fish during social viewing, but was reduced in partially isolated fish, perhaps representing some recovery during the 15 min of social interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D left: C vs Fi, p=6.3e−13 Mann-Whitney; C vs Pi, p=0.03 Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Anti-social fish exhibited increased freezing during social viewing regardless of rearing condition.
source: When we compared freezing behaviour of groups with similar social preference, we found, as expected, that anti-social fish exhibited increased freezing during social viewing regardless of rearing condition.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Pro-social fully isolated fish showed increased freezing during social viewing.
source: However, pro-social fully isolated fish also showed increased freezing during social viewing, suggesting that they were not engaged in typical social interaction, but rather remained immobile on the side with the conspecifics (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D right).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Pro-social fully isolated fish were not engaged in typical social interaction, but rather remained immobile on the side with the conspecifics.
source: However, pro-social fully isolated fish also showed increased freezing during social viewing, suggesting that they were not engaged in typical social interaction, but rather remained immobile on the side with the conspecifics (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D right).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: c-fos is an immediate early gene whose expression is associated with increased neural activity.
source: To test this hypothesis, we performed whole-brain two-photon imaging of c-fos expression, an immediate early gene whose expression is associated with increased neural activity (Herrera and Robertson, 1996), in juvenile brains following testing in the social preference assay.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The dorsal sub-region of the caudal hypothalamus was significantly activated in pro-social controls.
source: A dorsal sub-region was significantly activated in pro-social controls (Figure 2B and D: dHc - C (+S) vs C (nsc), p=0.007, Mann-Whitney)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2B and D.

claim: The dorsal sub-region of the caudal hypothalamus was inhibited in anti-social controls.
source: A dorsal sub-region was significantly activated in pro-social controls (Figure 2B and D: dHc - C (+S) vs C (nsc), p=0.007, Mann-Whitney), whereas it was inhibited, along with the adjacent ventral sub-region, in anti-social controls (Figure 2B and D: vHc - C (-S) vs C (nsc), p=0.003, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2B and D.

claim: The ventral sub-region of the caudal hypothalamus was inhibited in anti-social controls.
source: A dorsal sub-region was significantly activated in pro-social controls (Figure 2B and D: dHc - C (+S) vs C (nsc), p=0.007, Mann-Whitney), whereas it was inhibited, along with the adjacent ventral sub-region, in anti-social controls (Figure 2B and D: vHc - C (-S) vs C (nsc), p=0.003, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2B and D.

claim: The caudal hypothalamus is known to express high levels of serotonin and dopamine, as well as glutamate and histamine.
source: The caudal hypothalamus is known to express high levels of serotonin and dopamine, as well as glutamate and histamine (Filippi et al., 2010; Kaslin and Panula, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A segregation into distinct dorsal and ventral areas of the caudal hypothalamus has been shown for tyrosine hydroxylase 1 and 2 (Th1 and Th2).
source: Furthermore, a segregation into distinct dorsal and ventral areas of the caudal hypothalamus has already been shown for some of these markers, such as tyrosine hydroxylase 1 and 2, (Th1 and Th2) (Yamamoto et al., 2010) and we confirmed these previous results with immunostaining (Figure 2C left)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and Figure 2C.

claim: A segregation into distinct dorsal and ventral areas of the caudal hypothalamus has been shown for the dopamine and serotonin transporters, DAT and slc6a4b.
source: Furthermore, a segregation into distinct dorsal and ventral areas of the caudal hypothalamus has already been shown for some of these markers, such as tyrosine hydroxylase 1 and 2, (Th1 and Th2) (Yamamoto et al., 2010) and we confirmed these previous results with immunostaining (Figure 2C left), as well as for the dopamine and serotonin transporters, DAT and slc6a4b (Figure 2C right) (Filippi et al., 2010; Lillesaar, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and Figure 2C.

claim: Changes in serotonin and dopamine levels have been widely documented in response to social interaction.
source: Changes in serotonin and dopamine levels have been widely documented in response to social interaction (Scerbina et al., 2012), viewing social cues (Saif et al., 2013), and social isolation (Huang et al., 2015; Shams et al., 2018; Shams et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Changes in serotonin and dopamine levels have been widely documented in response to viewing social cues.
source: Changes in serotonin and dopamine levels have been widely documented in response to social interaction (Scerbina et al., 2012), viewing social cues (Saif et al., 2013), and social isolation (Huang et al., 2015; Shams et al., 2018; Shams et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Changes in serotonin and dopamine levels have been widely documented in response to social isolation.
source: Changes in serotonin and dopamine levels have been widely documented in response to social interaction (Scerbina et al., 2012), viewing social cues (Saif et al., 2013), and social isolation (Huang et al., 2015; Shams et al., 2018; Shams et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The serotoninergic system has been linked to stress and arousal.
source: While the serotoninergic system has been linked to stress and arousal (Backström and Winberg, 2017), the dopamine circuitry has been shown to regulate the reward system underlying social behaviour (Teles et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The dopamine circuitry has been shown to regulate the reward system underlying social behaviour.
source: While the serotoninergic system has been linked to stress and arousal (Backström and Winberg, 2017), the dopamine circuitry has been shown to regulate the reward system underlying social behaviour (Teles et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The caudal hypothalamus could be crucial in regulating social preference.
source: Since the caudal hypothalamus expresses both of these neurotransmitters, and our data demonstrate a pattern of activation/inhibition that is distinct for pro- and anti-social fish, then this area could be crucial in regulating social preference.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the data.

claim: Only anti-social control fish showed a significant change in the ventral preoptic area.
source: Our data showed a similar activation pattern for anti-social and pro-social fish characterised by a small increase in the dorsal preoptic area (dPa) and a small decrease in the ventral preoptic area (vPa). However, only anti-social control fish showed a significant change in the ventral area (Figure 2B and D: C (-S) vs C (nsc), vPa p=0.003, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2B and D.

claim: The activation of the preoptic area during social behaviour is consistent with previous literature in a number of species.
source: The activation of the preoptic area during social behaviour is consistent with previous literature in a number of species (O'Connell and Hofmann, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The preoptic area has been shown to express several neuropeptides involved in social behaviour such as arginine/vasotocin and oxytocin.
source: This area has been shown to express several neuropeptides involved in social behaviour such as arginine/vasotocin and oxytocin (Heinrichs et al., 2009; Herget and Ryu, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Oxytocin does not seem to be responsible for social interaction.
source: It was recently shown that oxytocin does not seem to be responsible for social interaction (Ribeiro et al., 2019) as mutants for oxytocin receptors shows no alteration in social preference, but rather reduced social recognition.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Mutants for oxytocin receptors show no alteration in social preference, but rather reduced social recognition.
source: It was recently shown that oxytocin does not seem to be responsible for social interaction (Ribeiro et al., 2019) as mutants for oxytocin receptors shows no alteration in social preference, but rather reduced social recognition.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Injections of oxytocin do not have any effect on shoaling and interaction.
source: Furthermore, injections of oxytocin do not have any effect on shoaling and interaction (Langen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The neuropeptide vasotocin has been shown to have a specific effect on reducing social interaction.
source: The neuropeptide vasotocin, instead, has been shown to have a specific effect on reducing social interaction (Langen et al., 2015) and not shoaling behaviour.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Vasotocin does not affect shoaling behaviour.
source: The neuropeptide vasotocin, instead, has been shown to have a specific effect on reducing social interaction (Langen et al., 2015) and not shoaling behaviour.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Vasotocin has been shown to be involved in aggression.
source: This neuropeptide has also been shown to be involved in aggression (Teles et al., 2016) and stress by stimulating cortisol release.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Vasotocin has been shown to be involved in stress by stimulating cortisol release.
source: This neuropeptide has also been shown to be involved in aggression (Teles et al., 2016) and stress by stimulating cortisol release.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: C-fos functional maps of anti-social fully isolated fish revealed a completely different activity profile than their anti-social sibling controls.
source: Contrary to our hypothesis, c-fos functional maps of anti-social fully isolated fish (Figure 2B: Fi (-S)) revealed a completely different activity profile than their anti-social sibling controls (Figure 2B: C (-S)).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2B.

claim: The ventral sub-region of the caudal hypothalamus (vHc) of Fi (-S) fish was not inactivated.
source: The ventral sub-region of the caudal hypothalamus (vHc) of Fi (-S) fish was not inactivated, while the preoptic area was strongly activated in both the dorsal (dPa) and the ventral (vPa) regions, but significantly only in the dorsal (Figure 2B and D: Fi (-S) vs Fi (nsc), p=0.006 dPa; p=0.07 vPa, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2B and D.

claim: The preoptic area of Fi (-S) fish was strongly activated in both the dorsal (dPa) and the ventral (vPa) regions, but significantly only in the dorsal.
source: The ventral sub-region of the caudal hypothalamus (vHc) of Fi (-S) fish was not inactivated, while the preoptic area was strongly activated in both the dorsal (dPa) and the ventral (vPa) regions, but significantly only in the dorsal (Figure 2B and D: Fi (-S) vs Fi (nsc), p=0.006 dPa; p=0.07 vPa, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2B and D.

claim: Pro-social fully isolated fish showed a similar activation to pro-social controls in the caudal hypothalamus.
source: Furthermore, the pro-social fully isolated fish (Figure 2B: Fi (+S)), who exhibited an increase of freezes and reduced motility compared to control fish when viewing conspecifics, showed a similar activation to pro-social controls in the caudal hypothalamus, but increased activity in the dorsal preoptic area.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Pro-social fully isolated fish showed increased activity in the dorsal preoptic area.
source: Furthermore, the pro-social fully isolated fish (Figure 2B: Fi (+S)), who exhibited an increase of freezes and reduced motility compared to control fish when viewing conspecifics, showed a similar activation to pro-social controls in the caudal hypothalamus, but increased activity in the dorsal preoptic area.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2B.

claim: The preoptic area was activated differently in pro-social and anti-social isolated fish, with only the dorsal preoptic area strongly activated in the pro-social group.
source: Interestingly, the preoptic area was activated differently in pro-social and anti-social isolated fish, with only the dorsal preoptic area strongly activated in the pro-social group (Figure 2B and D: Fi (+S) vs Fi, p=0.04 vPa, p=0.002 dPa, Man-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2B and D.

claim: Long social isolation causes abnormal neural responses during viewing of social cues.
source: These data suggest that long social isolation causes abnormal neural responses during viewing of social cues.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Anti- and pro-social fish exposed to a brief isolation for only 48 hr prior to testing showed similar functional activity changes to fully isolated fish, albeit less strong.
source: Furthermore, anti- and pro-social fish exposed to a brief isolation for only 48 hr prior to testing, showed similar functional activity changes to fully isolated fish, albeit less strong (Figure 2B and D: Pi (-S) vs Pi (nsc), p=0.18 dHc; p=0.28 vHc; p=0.04 vPa; p=0.04 dPa, Mann-Whitney; Figure 2B and D: Pi (+S) vs Pi (nsc), p=0.17 dHc; p=0.05 vHc; p=0.007 vPa; p=0.006 dPa).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2B and D.

claim: Short term isolation is enough to induce brain activity changes similar to those observed following complete isolation.
source: Together with the behavioural data, this finding supports the idea that short term isolation is enough to induce brain activity changes similar to those observed following complete isolation, and strikingly different than those observed in anti-social controls.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: There was a significant increase in c-fos activity in the optic tectum of isolated fish not exposed to social cues.
source: When we directly compared the normalised c-fos functional brain maps of isolated and control fish that were not exposed to social cues during the assay (Figure 3A), we found a significant increase in two interesting areas; one associated with visual processing, the optic tectum, [McDowell et al., 2004]), and one involved in stress responses, the posterior tuberal nucleus (Ziv et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3A and citations to previous work.

claim: There was a significant increase in c-fos activity in the posterior tuberal nucleus of isolated fish not exposed to social cues.
source: When we directly compared the normalised c-fos functional brain maps of isolated and control fish that were not exposed to social cues during the assay (Figure 3A), we found a significant increase in two interesting areas; one associated with visual processing, the optic tectum, [McDowell et al., 2004]), and one involved in stress responses, the posterior tuberal nucleus (Ziv et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3A and citations to previous work.

claim: The optic tectum is associated with visual processing.
source: When we directly compared the normalised c-fos functional brain maps of isolated and control fish that were not exposed to social cues during the assay (Figure 3A), we found a significant increase in two interesting areas; one associated with visual processing, the optic tectum, [McDowell et al., 2004]), and one involved in stress responses, the posterior tuberal nucleus (Ziv et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The posterior tuberal nucleus is involved in stress responses.
source: When we directly compared the normalised c-fos functional brain maps of isolated and control fish that were not exposed to social cues during the assay (Figure 3A), we found a significant increase in two interesting areas; one associated with visual processing, the optic tectum, [McDowell et al., 2004]), and one involved in stress responses, the posterior tuberal nucleus (Ziv et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In pro-social control fish, viewing social cues resulted in a significant increase of neuronal activity in the optic tectum.
source: In pro-social control fish, viewing social cues resulted in a significant increase of neuronal activity in the optic tectum (Figure 3B top: C (+S) vs C (nsc), p=0.004 Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3B.

claim: In fully isolated fish, there was already increased neuronal activity in the optic tectum in the absence of social cues.
source: However, in fully isolated fish, there was already increased neuronal activity in the optic tectum in the absence of social cues (Figure 3B top: Fi (nsc) vs C (nsc), p=0.0004, Mann-Whitney), suggesting that isolation increases visual sensitivity, as previously reported in humans (Cacioppo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis, Figure 3B, and a citation to previous work.

claim: Isolation increases visual sensitivity.
source: However, in fully isolated fish, there was already increased neuronal activity in the optic tectum in the absence of social cues (Figure 3B top: Fi (nsc) vs C (nsc), p=0.0004, Mann-Whitney), suggesting that isolation increases visual sensitivity, as previously reported in humans (Cacioppo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the data and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The increased sensitivity of fully isolated fish not presented with social cues was weaker in partially isolated fish.
source: This increased sensitivity of fully isolated fish not presented with social cues was weaker in partially isolated fish (Figure 3B top: Pi (nsc) vs C (nsc), p=0.03, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3B.

claim: A much larger increase in tectal activity was observed when pro-social partially isolated fish viewed conspecifics, revealing that some visual sensitization had occurred.
source: However, a much larger increase in tectal activity was observed when pro-social partially isolated fish viewed conspecifics, revealing that some visual sensitization had occurred (Figure 3B top: Pi (+S) vs C (+S), p=0.0002, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3B.

claim: Increased tectal activity was present in both fully and partially isolated anti-social fish.
source: In addition, increased tectal activity was also present in both fully and partially isolated anti-social fish (Figure 3B top: Fi (-S) vs C (-S), p=0.048; Pi (-S) vs C (-S), p=0.005, Mann-Whitney), even though these fish largely avoided the chamber with visual access to conspecifics.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3B.

claim: Full isolation caused a significant increase in posterior tuberal nucleus activity in the absence of social cues.
source: Full isolation caused a significant increase in posterior tuberal nucleus activity in the absence of social cues (Figure 3B bottom: Fi (nsc) vs C (nsc), p=0.015, Mann-Whitney)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3B.

claim: Full isolation caused a significant increase in posterior tuberal nucleus activity in both anti-social and pro-social fish exposed to social cues.
source: Full isolation caused a significant increase in posterior tuberal nucleus activity in the absence of social cues (Figure 3B bottom: Fi (nsc) vs C (nsc), p=0.015, Mann-Whitney) and in both anti-social and pro-social fish exposed to social cues (Figure 3B bottom: Fi (+S) vs C (+S), p=0.003; Fi (-S) vs C (-S), p=0.016, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3B.

claim: Following partial isolation, posterior tuberal nucleus activity was not increased in the absence of social cues.
source: Following partial isolation, posterior tuberal nucleus activity was not increased in the absence of social cues (Figure 3B bottom: Pi (nsc) vs C (nsc), p=0.29, Mann-Whitney)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3B.

claim: Following partial isolation, posterior tuberal nucleus activity was only slightly increased in pro-social fish.
source: Following partial isolation, posterior tuberal nucleus activity was not increased in the absence of social cues (Figure 3B bottom: Pi (nsc) vs C (nsc), p=0.29, Mann-Whitney), only slightly in pro-social fish (Figure 3B bottom: Pi (+S) vs C (+S), p=0.018)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3B.

claim: Following partial isolation, posterior tuberal nucleus activity was significantly increased in anti-social fish.
source: Following partial isolation, posterior tuberal nucleus activity was not increased in the absence of social cues (Figure 3B bottom: Pi (nsc) vs C (nsc), p=0.29, Mann-Whitney), only slightly in pro-social fish (Figure 3B bottom: Pi (+S) vs C (+S), p=0.018), but significantly so in anti-social fish (Figure 3B bottom: Pi (-S) vs C (-S), p=0.0005).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3B.

claim: Isolation initially heightens sensitivity to social stimuli.
source: Given these results from the optic tectum and posterior tuberal nucleus, we propose that isolation initially heightens sensitivity to social stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the data.

claim: When prolonged, heightened sensitivity to social stimuli results in an increase of stress and anxiety levels during social viewing that leads to an aversion for social stimuli.
source: However, when prolonged, this heightened sensitivity results in an increase of stress and anxiety levels during social viewing that leads to an aversion for social stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the data.

claim: Buspirone is an agonist of the auto-inhibitory 5HT1A receptor.
source: To test our hypothesis that reducing anxiety could reverse the anti-social behaviour observed in isolated zebrafish, we acutely treated control and partially isolated fish with Buspirone, an agonist of the auto-inhibitory 5HT1A receptor.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The caudal hypothalamus and the preoptic area strongly express Htr1ab receptors, one of the two orthologues of the 5HT1A receptor.
source: The choice of Buspirone was supported by the changes in activity observed in the caudal hypothalamus of isolated fish, and by the fact that the caudal hypothalamus and the preoptic area strongly express Htr1ab receptors, one of the two orthologues of the 5HT1A receptor (Norton et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Buspirone has been shown to reduce anxiety in humans, mice, and zebrafish.
source: Buspirone has been shown to reduce anxiety in humans, mice, and zebrafish (Bencan et al., 2009; Lalonde and Strazielle, 2010; Lau et al., 2011; Patel and Hillard, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Buspirone has been shown to enhance social interaction of rats.
source: While it is not fully understood how Buspirone reduces anxiety, it has been shown to enhance social interaction of rats (File and Seth, 2003; Gould et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Buspirone has been shown to enhance sociability of zebrafish.
source: While it is not fully understood how Buspirone reduces anxiety, it has been shown to enhance social interaction of rats (File and Seth, 2003; Gould et al., 2011), sociability of zebrafish (Barba-Escobedo and Gould, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Buspirone has been shown to reduce social phobia in humans.
source: While it is not fully understood how Buspirone reduces anxiety, it has been shown to enhance social interaction of rats (File and Seth, 2003; Gould et al., 2011), sociability of zebrafish (Barba-Escobedo and Gould, 2012), and reduce social phobia in humans (Schneier et al., 1993; van Vliet et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Acute exposure to Buspirone in control fish resulted in a small significant increase in social preference relative to untreated controls.
source: We first tested the effects of acute exposure to Buspirone in control fish, and, as expected, we observed a small significant increase in social preference relative to untreated controls, however, a population of ~10% anti-social fish remained (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; C (no drug) vs C (30 µM), p=0.01, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A population of ~10% anti-social fish remained after acute exposure to Buspirone in control fish.
source: We first tested the effects of acute exposure to Buspirone in control fish, and, as expected, we observed a small significant increase in social preference relative to untreated controls, however, a population of ~10% anti-social fish remained (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; C (no drug) vs C (30 µM), p=0.01, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Acute drug treatment with Buspirone was sufficient to reverse the anti-social phenotype caused by isolation.
source: Remarkably, the acute drug treatment was sufficient in both concentrations to reverse the anti-social phenotype caused by isolation (Figure 4A; Pi vs Pi (Buspirone 30 µM and 50 µM combined), p=2.56 e-05, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 4A.

claim: Isolated fish treated with Buspirone, while initially anti-social, would rapidly recover normal social preference behaviour within the first 5 min of exposure to social cues.
source: We found that the isolated fish treated with Buspirone, while initially anti-social, would rapidly recover normal social preference behaviour within the first 5 min of exposure to social cues (Figure 4B: C vs Pi (Buspirone), p=0.016, first minute; p=0.37, fourth minute, Mann-Whitney).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 4B.

claim: The VPIs of untreated isolated fish remained significantly lower than controls throughout the entire session.
source: In contrast, the VPIs of untreated isolated fish remained significantly lower than controls throughout the entire session.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: The activity of isolated fish treated with Buspirone was already at the level of controls from the start of the social viewing session.
source: Notably, the activity of isolated fish treated with Buspirone was already at the level of controls from the start of the social viewing session (Figure 4B: C vs Pi (Buspirone), p=0.31, first minute, Mann-Whitney)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 4B.

claim: The recovery of normal movement activity, possibly as a result of reduced anxiety, precedes the recovery of normal social preference.
source: Notably, the activity of isolated fish treated with Buspirone was already at the level of controls from the start of the social viewing session (Figure 4B: C vs Pi (Buspirone), p=0.31, first minute, Mann-Whitney), which suggests that the recovery of normal movement activity, possibly as a result of reduced anxiety, precedes the recovery of normal social preference.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Buspirone's impact on the rate of recovery of social preference indicates that it may do so by reducing anxiety, perhaps at the level of the preoptic and/or caudal hypothalamic area, allowing circuit plasticity to down-regulate the hypersensitivity to social stimuli acquired during the isolation period.
source: Therefore, Buspirone's impact on the rate of recovery of social preference indicates that it may do so by reducing anxiety, perhaps at the level of the preoptic and/or caudal hypothalamic area, allowing circuit plasticity to down-regulate the hypersensitivity to social stimuli acquired during the isolation period.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Lonely fish, which have been isolated from social cues and show anti-social behaviour, have a completely different functional response to social stimuli than loner fish, anti-social fish found in the normal population.
source: In summary, our results demonstrate that lonely fish, which have been isolated from social cues and show anti-social behaviour, have a completely different functional response to social stimuli than loner fish, anti-social fish found in the normal population.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings.

claim: The functional changes caused by social deprivation are consistent with an increase in anxiety resulting from hyper-sensitization to social stimuli, similar to the effects of isolation on humans.
source: In addition, the functional changes caused by social deprivation are consistent with an increase in anxiety resulting from hyper-sensitization to social stimuli, similar to the effects of isolation on humans.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings.

claim: Isolation's effects in zebrafish could be reversed with an existing anxiolytic drug that acts on the monoaminergic system.
source: We could reverse isolation's effects in zebrafish with an existing anxiolytic drug that acts on the monoaminergic system.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings.

claim: Zebrafish will provide a powerful new tool for studying the impact of loneliness (isolation) on brain function and exploring different strategies for reducing, or even reversing, its harm.
source: Zebrafish will thus provide a powerful new tool for studying the impact of loneliness (isolation) on brain function and exploring different strategies for reducing, or even reversing, its harm.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Social preference behaviour is the drive for individuals to identify and approach members of their own species.
source: Social preference behaviour, the drive for individuals to identify and approach members of their own species (Rogers-Carter et al., 2018; Winslow, 2003), is a fundamental component of all social behaviour.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Social preference behaviour is a fundamental component of all social behaviour.
source: Social preference behaviour, the drive for individuals to identify and approach members of their own species (Rogers-Carter et al., 2018; Winslow, 2003), is a fundamental component of all social behaviour.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Loneliness is undesired isolation from social interaction.
source: Loneliness, undesired isolation from social interaction, has been linked to a reduction in social preference (Engeszer et al., 2004; Shams et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a definition.

claim: Dissected brains were imaged with the dorsal surface down (bottom-up) to achieve clear views of the ventral brain structures that have been previously implicated in the social brain network.
source: Dissected brains were imaged with the dorsal surface down (bottom-up) to achieve clear views of the ventral brain structures that have been previously implicated in the social brain network (Figure 2A, also see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail.

claim: Volumes of 1.5 mm x 1.5 mm x 700 µm, with a voxel size of 1 × 1×3 µm, were acquired from 135 zebrafish brains across all experimental groups and registered to a reference brain.
source: Volumes of 1.5 mm x 1.5 mm x 700 µm, with a voxel size of 1 × 1×3 µm, were acquired from 135 zebrafish brains across all experimental groups and registered to a reference brain (Marquart et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail and supported by a citation.
